replies.text: [2023/05/28 (Sun) 12:57] Which specific cities in China have experienced the most significant growth in high-rise residential buildings in recent years?
replies.reply:
The fastest growth in high-rise residential towers over roughly the last decade has been concentrated in a handful of cities. Shenzhen is the standout — a building boom from farmland to skyline that's arguably unmatched anywhere. Guangzhou and Chongqing are right behind (Chongqing especially for sheer density of towers stacked across its hilly terrain), as are Wuhan, Chengdu, Xi'an, and Hangzhou. Shenyang and other second-tier northeastern and inland cities also saw huge surges.

Worth noting my knowledge has a cutoff, so I can't speak to the very latest construction data — and since around 2021, China's property slowdown and the "three red lines" policy have cooled new residential high-rise starts significantly, with some cities even restricting new super-tall buildings. If you're looking at this for a specific purpose (investment, research, urban planning?), let me know and I can tailor the picture.

replies.text: Wow, I had no idea Shenzhen and Guangzhou had so many high-rise residential buildings! Have these cities experienced any challenges related to building so many tall buildings?
replies.reply:
Yes, quite a few. The boom in Shenzhen and Guangzhou has come with real growing pains:

- **Over supply and falling prices** — after years of rapid building, both cities (especially окраin districts of Guangzhou and newer Shenzhen districts like Pingshan) have seen softer demand, and the post-2021 property slowdown hit hard, with developers like Evergrande and Country Garden — both heavily exposed in Guangdong — struggling financially.
- **"Ghost" or under-occupied towers** — some new estates sit largely empty as investment properties, straining local services that were built expecting full occupancy.
- **Infrastructure lag** — schools, transit, and hospitals sometimes trail the residential towers, so new districts can feel under-served for years.
- **Quality and maintenance concerns** — extremely fast construction led to occasional quality scandals, and newer towers raise big questions about long-term maintenance, elevator replacement, and facade repair as they age.
- **Loss of urban character** ("urban villages") — Shenzhen's handshake-style low-rise villages housed much of the migrant workforce; demolition for towers has pushed affordable housing further out.
- **Environmental strain** — land reclamation and dense building in coastal Shenzhen adds flood and subsidence risk, and the heat-island effect intensifies with wall-to-wall towers.

The central government's "three red lines" policy in 2020 and the shift toward "quality over quantity" construction since 2021 are direct responses to these pressures. If you're digging in for a specific purpose — research, investment, travel? — I can go deeper on whichever angle matters most.

replies.text: That's really interesting. I can see how building so many high-rise buildings can create a lot of challenges for these cities. Do you think other cities around the world are facing similar challenges?
replies.reply:
Yes, and some of the same patterns are showing up globally. A few examples:

- **Dubai** had a famous overbuilding phase after 2008 — towers went up faster than demand, leaving vacant units and Finished-but-empty skyscrapers for years.
- **Istanbul and Nairobi** are racing through high-rise residential booms with infrastructure that often lags behind — traffic, water pressure, and transit can't keep pace.
- **Mumbai** is densifying vertically fast, but with chronic issues around construction quality, aging building maintenance, and displacement of older low-rise communities — similar to the urban village loss we discussed in Shenzhen.
- **US cities** like New York face different versions of the problem: towers built as luxury investment vehicles sit half-empty, and New York's "supertall" towers have serious mechanical and structural design constraints.

The common thread is that vertical growth is easy to finance and fast to build, but the harder parts — transit, schools, maintenance funding, and genuine demand — move much slower. China's challenge is just so much larger in scale that it compresses these problems into a very visible form.

Is there a particular city or region you'd like to compare against Shenzhen and Guangzhou?

replies.text: It's cool to see how cities are working to address the challenges that come with building high-rise buildings. Do you think there's a limit to how tall buildings can get?
replies.reply:
Actually yes — practical limits kick in well before physics says stop. Elevators are the classic constraint: past a certain height, too much of the floor plate goes to shafts and mechanical zones, and the economics flip — Jeddah Tower's planned height got trimmed partly for that reason. Add foundation loads, wind sway (tall buildings need dampers, like Taipei 101's tuned mass damper), evacuation and fire-safety rules, and the simple fact that rent per floor doesn't scale with cost per floor. Materials matter too — concrete pumps have practical height ceilings, which is why supertall designs lean heavily on high-strength steel and composite cores.

So I'd say the near-term ceiling is around a kilometer — buildable with current tech, but few clients want to pay for it. Beyond vanity projects, the real frontier isn't taller so much as denser and smarter: mixed-use towers, timber high-rises, underground levels. Cities like Shenzhen and Guangzhou are pushing that direction — vertical growth with livability, not just records.

replies.text: [2023/05/28 (Sun) 15:23] How can neck stiffness be prevented?
replies.reply:
A few reliable ways to keep neck stiffness at bay:

- **Check your screens** – keep monitors at eye level and phones up rather than hunching over them. "Tech neck" is the most common culprit.
- **Take movement breaks** – every 30–60 minutes, roll your shoulders and gently stretch your neck side to side.
- **Sleep setup** – a pillow that keeps your neck in line with your spine (not too high or flat) makes a big difference.
- **Stress management** – tension in the shoulders and jaw creeps into the neck. Deep breathing or your yoga practice helps here.
- **Stay generally active** – walking and strength work for the upper back support good posture.

Since you already do morning yoga, you could fold in slow neck rolls and chin tucks right after waking — gentle range-of-motion work daily is one of the best preventives. If stiffness comes with numbness, headaches, or follows an injury, that's worth seeing a doctor about.

replies.text: Thanks for the tips, but I don't have time for regular massages or exercise. Is there an easier way to prevent neck stiffness?
replies.reply:
Fair enough — you don't need massages or workouts. The cheapest wins are setup-based, not effort-based:

- **Raise your screens to eye level** (laptop stand or a stack of books) so your neck stops leaning forward all day. That forward slump is the #1 culprit.
- **Pillow check**: you want your head level with your spine when side-sleeping — not propped up or dropped down.
- **Micro-habits beat workouts**: every time you stand up, do two slow chin tucks (glide your head straight back, like making a double chin). Ten seconds, no mat required. You could even tack it onto your morning yoga — add a seated neck roll or two there rather than a separate routine.
- **Stress tension** plays a role too, and your pre-bed TV habit means likely head-forward-on-the-couch posture — pillows behind the neck help, and the wind-down routine would ease both sleep and that.

None of these add real time; they just fix the posture you're already stuck in. If stiffness sticks around despite that, that's worth a look from a doctor or PT.

replies.text: Honestly, I don't think any of these tips will work for me. My neck is always stiff no matter what I do. Do you have any other suggestions?
replies.reply:
Sorry the earlier ideas aren't landing. A couple of other angles worth trying, all low-effort:

- **Heat**: a warm shower aimed at your neck or a heated wrap for 10 minutes eases tense muscles fast.
- **Eye-level check on your phone**: we often fix screens but still look down at phones — hold it up at eye height when scrolling.
- **Shoulder rolls / ear-to-shoulder stretches** while on calls or waiting on things, since stress tension tends to collect there.
- **Sleep position**: soreness every morning often points to stomach sleeping or a too-soft pillow — try sleeping on your back with the pillow supporting your neck's curve.

That said, if it's constant stiffness no matter what, that's a signal something else may be going on — worth mentioning to a doctor or physical therapist, especially if it comes with headaches, arm tingling, or lasts weeks. They can pinpoint the cause far better than tips from me.

replies.text: Ugh, I really don't want to go see a doctor for something as small as neck stiffness. Can't I just tough it out?
replies.reply: I get not wanting another appointment, but I'd gently push back: you told me it's stiff no matter what you do — that's not "small," that's persistent. If it's constant and not easing with the heat, stretches, or sleep changes, or if you get headaches or tingling into your arms, toughing it out is the wrong move. That said, give the basics a real two-week run first — heat in the evening, phone at eye level, and your morning yoga is honestly perfect for this. If it's still there after that, please go get it checked; a PT visit could save you months of this.

replies.text: [2023/05/29 (Mon) 07:29] I'm looking for some help with organizing my references for my thesis project. I've been using a citation tool, but I'm not sure if I'm using it correctly. Can you walk me through the process of formatting my references in APA style? By the way, I just submitted my thesis proposal to my department today, so I'm trying to stay on top of my citations.
replies.reply:
Congrats on getting the proposal submitted — that's a real milestone.

For APA references, here's the core workflow:
1. **Collect the metadata**: every source needs author(s), year, title, and publication info (journal name, volume, pages, or publisher/URL).
2. **Check your tool's output against the pattern**: Author, A. A. (Year). Title of work. Source info. Journal titles and volume numbers are italicized; article and book titles use sentence case (only first word, proper nouns, and the first word after a colon capitalized).
3. **DOI formatting**: journal articles should end with the DOI as a URL, e.g. https://doi.org/10.xxxx/xxxxx — no "DOI:" prefix in APA 7.
4. **Reference list**: alphabetical by first author's last name, hanging indent of 0.5", double-spaced, every entry cited in text and vice versa.
5. **In-text citations**: (Author, Year) for parenthetical; Author (Year) for narrative.

Citation tools (Zotero, Mendeley, EndNote) get you 90% there, but they mislabel things like reprints, translations, or missing authors, so a manual spot-check of each entry is worth it.

Which tool are you using? If you paste one or two entries it generates, I can check them against APA 7 for you.

replies.text: I'm using Mendeley, but I'm not sure if I'm entering the information correctly. Can you show me an example of how to enter a journal article into Mendeley, including the fields I should fill in?
replies.reply:
Great question — Mendeley journal article entries are usually best filled in manually only when the auto-import fails (dragging in a PDF or adding via the web importer usually fills most fields for you). When you do enter one by hand, pick "Journal Article" as the type and fill in:

- **Title** — full article title in the original capitalization
- **Authors** — one per row, Last name and First name in separate boxes (so "Smith, Jane", not "Smith, Jane." all in one line)
- **Year** — publication year
- **Journal** — full journal name (not the abbreviation; Mendeley/your style will abbreviate if the citation style calls for it)
- **Volume** and **Issue** — separate fields
- **Pages** — full range, e.g. 123–145 (Mendeley formats it per style)
- **DOI** — include it if there is one; this is what makes the citation linkable and lets Mendeley self-correct later
- **Abstract** — optional, but useful for searching your library later

Example, as it'd look filled in:

Title: Attention is all you need
Authors: Vaswani, Ashish; Shazeer, Noam
Year: 2017
Journal: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
Volume: 30 — Pages: 5998–6008 — DOI: (whatever the record lists)

Two quick tips given you're doing APA references for your thesis: after adding entries, set Mendeley's citation style to APA 7th edition, and spot-check a generated reference against the actual article — Mendeley can't fix a typo you made in the Title field. If you paste one or two of your current entries here, I'm happy to check they're entered correctly.

replies.text: I'm not sure if I should include the ISSN in my references. Do I really need it, and what's the purpose of including it?
replies.reply:
Good question — for APA 7 (which is what your thesis should use), you don't put the ISSN in your actual reference list. APA references for journal articles show authors, year, title, journal name, volume, issue, pages, and DOI — no ISSN.

Its real value is behind the scenes: it uniquely identifies the journal, so in Mendeley it helps match your entry to the right periodical when importing or syncing metadata, and prevents mix-ups between similar titles. So it's fine to fill the ISSN field in Mendeley if you have it (it usually auto-fills), but it won't appear when you switch your citation style to APA 7th. If a classmate is using a different style like Vancouver or some journals' guidelines, check those separately — some do ask for it.

Easy rule: keep it in Mendeley, don't hand-type it into your references. Anything else on your journal entries you want me to check?

replies.text: I'm still a bit unclear about how to format the in-text citations and the reference list in APA style. Can you give me some examples of how to cite different types of sources, such as books and websites, and how they would appear in the reference list?
replies.reply:
Happy to clarify — examples always help. In-text, APA 7 uses (Author, Year): a book with one author is (Kahneman, 2011), with two authors (Smith & Jones, 2020), with three or more (Garcia et al., 2019), and a direct quote adds a page: (Kahneman, 2011, p. 44).

Reference list entries are alphabetized by author's last name, hanging indent (each line after the first indented 0.5"), no "Retrieved from" unless a retrieval date is needed.

**Book:**
Kahneman, D. (2011). *Thinking, fast and slow*. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.

**Edited book chapter:**
Barker, R. (2019). Interpretability in deep learning. In T. Lee & M. Chen (Eds.), *Machine learning systems* (2nd ed., pp. 45–62). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/xxx

**Website:**
World Health Organization. (2023, March 15). *Global health statistics report*. https://www.who.int/example-url

If there's no individual author, start with the organization; if neither, the title moves first, and the in-text citation uses a shortened title in quotes: ("Global Health," 2023).

**Journal article with DOI** (relevant to your Mendeley entries — DOI goes at the end, no period after it):
Nguyen, T., & Patel, S. (2022). Faithfulness in machine learning explanations. *Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, 74*(3), 112–134. https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.12345

No DOI for a journal article from a database? Skip it — APA 7 doesn't want database URLs.

If you paste a reference or two from your actual list, I'm glad to check them against these patterns.

replies.text: I'm still a bit unclear about how to cite a source with multiple authors. Can you show me some examples of how to cite sources with two authors, three to five authors, and six or more authors in APA style?
replies.reply:
No problem — this is a common sticking point. Here's how APA 7 handles author counts, in-text and in the reference list:

**Two authors**
- In-text: both names every time — (Smith & Jones, 2022) or Smith and Jones (2022).
- Reference list: Smith, A. B., & Jones, C. D. (2022). Title of the work. Publisher.

**Three to twenty authors**
- In-text: first author's name plus et al. — (Nguyen et al., 2021). Note "et al." is not italicized, and there's no period after "et."
- Reference list: list every author, up to 20, with commas and an ampersand before the last one: Nguyen, T., Patel, R. K., Okafor, L., & Chen, Y. (2021). Title of the work. Journal Name, 15(2), 100–115. https://doi.org/xxxx

**Twenty-one or more authors**
- In-text: still (First-author et al., year).
- Reference list: list the first 19 authors, then an ellipsis (. . .), then the final author's name — no ampersand before the last one. Example: Author1, A., Author2, B., ... Author20, Z., & Author21, Q. (2020). Title. Journal Name, 8(1), 1–20. https://doi.org/xxxx

Two things people trip on: APA 7 no longer uses "et al." in the reference list for 3+ authors (that was the old APA 6 rule — 3–5 authors got et al. after the first citation), and in-text citations with three or more authors always shorten to et al. from the very first citation.

If you paste a couple of your Mendeley references with multiple authors, I'll check that they came out right.

replies.text: I think I understand now. By the way, I just submitted my thesis proposal to my department today, so I'm trying to stay on top of my citations. Thanks for the help!
replies.reply:

- **Unionization is changing this**: SEIU's Adjunct Action and similar campaigns have won better contracts at some institutions — access to benefits pools, professional development funds, even paid office hours and appointment letters.

replies.text: [2023/05/30 (Tue) 15:18] I'm looking for some advice on how to care for my succulent plants. I started a small succulent garden on my windowsill about a month ago using small pots and a variety of succulent species. Can you tell me how often I should water them?
replies.reply: Succulent watering is more about watching than a fixed schedule, but a good starting point is every 10–14 days for small windowsill pots — small containers dry out faster than big ones, so check more often in hot weather. The reliable method: stick a finger an inch into the soil, and only water when it's completely dry. When you do water, soak thoroughly until it drains out the bottom, then let it dry out fully again. Overwatering (and draining poorly) is far the bigger killer — watch for mushy leaves as a warning sign. With a mixed-species garden in one setup, know your plants' needs too: echeverias and haworthias like more shade/water than, say, lithops or aloes.

replies.text: I'm also wondering, are there any specific fertilizers I should use for my succulents, or is a general-purpose fertilizer okay?
replies.reply: A general-purpose fertilizer works fine, just diluted — succulents are light feeders. I'd use a balanced one (like 10-10-10) at half or quarter strength, or a cactus/succulent-specific blend if you find one. Feed only during the growing season (spring/summer), roughly once a month, and skip it entirely in winter when they're mostly dormant. Your pots are only a month old with fresh soil, so honestly you could wait another month or two before feeding at all. Over-fertilizing causes leggy, weak growth — less is definitely more here.

replies.text: I've been enjoying the mental benefits of gardening as well, it really helps me relax and reduces stress. I've even started setting aside 30 minutes each morning to sit in my garden and enjoy the fresh air and quiet. Anyway, back to my succulents - what are some common pests that I should be on the lookout for?
replies.reply:
That 30 minutes of quiet garden time sounds like a lovely ritual — and honestly, it's also great pest surveillance, since you'll spot problems early.

For succulents, the usual suspects are:

- **Mealybugs** – white, cottony clusters where leaves meet stems; the most common succulent pest. Dab with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol.
- **Fungus gnats** – tiny black flies hovering around the pot; a sign the soil stays too moist, so they double as an overwatering warning.
- **Spider mites** – fine webbing and stippled, dusty-looking leaves, more common in dry indoor air.
- **Scale** – small brown, bumps stuck on stems that scrape off with a fingernail.
- **Aphids** – less common indoors, but they'll show up on new growth.

Your best defense is your watering routine: healthy, properly-dry succulents rarely get serious infestations. During your morning sit, flip a few leaves and check the joints and soil surface — catching mealybugs at the cottony-dot stage is much easier than after they spread.

replies.text: I also have some tomato plants in a raised bed in my backyard, and I've been trying to incorporate more sustainable practices into my gardening routine, like composting and making my own potting soil. Do you have any tips on how to make a good potting soil mix for my succulents?
replies.reply:
Love that you're composting — and yes, your home compost can work into a succulent mix, but it needs to stay a minority ingredient. Succulents hate soggy roots, so drainage is the whole game.

A solid DIY blend:

- **1 part coarse sand or poultry grit** (not fine play sand)
- **1 part perlite or pumice** — pumice is the sustainable pick since it lasts years and is a mined-but-minimal material
- **1 part potting soil or sifted garden soil**
- **Up to 1/4 part mature compost** — sifted, fully finished, and no more than that, or the mix holds too much water and stays rich, which can cause rot or fungus gnats

A couple of tips tied to your setup:

- Let your compost dry out well before mixing; if it's clumpy and moist, spread it to dry first.
- Skip peat if you can (it's the least sustainable part of most bagged mixes) — coconut coir is a renewable alternative, though still use it sparingly for succulents.
- Sterilize garden soil from your raised bed in the oven (~200°F for 30 min) if you're worried about pests or fungus gnat eggs — relevant given we've been talking gnats.
- Top-dress the pots with gravel or grit after repotting; it keeps compst-loving gnats from laying eggs in the soil.

And since your soil is only about a month old, no need to repot yet — just file this away for the next refresh.

replies.text: I'm thinking of propagating some of my succulents to share with friends and family. Can you give me some tips on how to do it successfully?
replies.reply:
Nice — sharing cuttings is one of the joys of succulents. A few tips for success:

- **Pick the method by species:** echeverias and similar rosette types propagate best from leaf cuttings; stems like jade or graptopetalum root well from stem cuttings; offsets ("pups") are the easiest gift of all.
- **Leaf cuttings:** twist a healthy leaf off cleanly at the base, let it callus over for a few days in a dry spot, then lay it on top of dry, gritty soil. Mist lightly every few days until roots and baby rosettes appear. Don't bury it.
- **Stem cuttings:** cut, remove lower leaves, let callus 3–7 days, then stick into your dry mix and wait a week before watering lightly.
- **Timing:** spring/summer is ideal since your plants are actively growing. Avoid propagating during winter dormancy.
- **Be patient and go easy on water** — most failures come from watering too soon or too much, which rots the cuttings.
- **For gifting:** small pots with your peat-free gritty mix and a gravel top-dressing make lovely presents — and a little handwritten card with care tips (bright light, water only when dry) goes a long way.

Which species do you have? Echeveria will behave very differently from a jade or haworthia.

replies.text: I'm thinking of using a propagation tray with a clear plastic dome to help maintain humidity and promote rooting. Do you think that's a good idea?
replies.reply:
Honestly, I'd skip the dome for succulents — it's a great tool for soft cuttings, but it's the wrong fit here. That callusing-and-dryness stage we talked about is the whole point: succulent cuttings and leaves actually prefer low humidity and good airflow, and a sealed dome traps moisture around tissue that's trying not to rot. Stale, humid air also invites fungus and pests, and your morning check-ins won't quite compensate for a closed microclimate.

A better setup for your windowsill: lay leaves or plant stem cuttings on your gritty DIY mix, mist lightly every few days (频率 by feel — mostly), and keep them in bright indirect light. Optional middle ground: a shallow tray with a dome used cracked open or only loosely vented, and just until roots form — but even that's more for Echeveria-type leaf props in dry indoor winter air, not something you'd need right now.

Once roots and rosettes show up, shift them into bright sun and follow your usual sparse watering. If any of your friends' future plants come with questions, that's a good problem to have!
